Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus inspired local masking, allowing task-independent predetermined graphs, even with sparsity rates as low as 4\%. We introduce locality-masked RNNs and make several breakthroughs, demonstrating these models match or outperform traditional RNNs in both training efficiency and data requirements. We examine locality-masked LSTM and fully connected RNN variations, and also explore an alternative, graph-masking approach. Furthermore, we show our models successfully replicate known RNN challenges and in addition, develop the first RNN algorithm for solving the well-known vector permutation problem.

We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results contribute to an understanding of the length of anticommutative algebras in further study.

Active galactic nuclei with exceptionally powerful radio signals are among the brightest known celestial sources, spanning across a wide range of wavelengths. These powerful jets from supermassive black holes can significantly influence the evolution of their surrounding galaxies, including the growth of supermassive black holes. In the radio spectrum, these jets can be observed on various scales, but their X-ray and gamma-ray emissions are typically confined to smaller scales, typically within a few hundred parsecs of the black hole. Recent observations at very high energies have revealed that some radio jets can extend far into galactic halos, reaching up to hundreds of kiloparsecs. In this study, we analyze the X-ray and gamma-ray emissions of double-lobed radio sources located within galactic halos. We selected 22 powerful radio sources located far from their central galaxies and compared their high-energy emissions to those of their local interstellar medium. Our findings show significant high-energy emissions towards the directions of their galactic halos, corresponding to large-angle jets. In particular, we found six sources with high-energy emissions along their galactic halos that can be attributed to their jets. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that these high-energy emissions could be the result of relativistic electrons interacting with dense regions within the galactic halo, particularly in the case of 3C 444 where we identify possible counterparts for two extended sources. Our findings support the notion that these high-energy emissions along galactic halos are a common feature of powerful radio sources

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$. We
re-derive the York action, which arises from a $1/c^2$ expansion, in a way that
is independent of the foliation's choice. Additionally, we show that a $1/c^2$
correction to the Hamiltonian derived from the York action results in the same
equations of motion as those obtained from a $1/c^2$ modified Einstein equations.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed feature extends descriptor modules to account for contrast reversal, doubling its potential outputs while maintaining computational efficiency. It offers more nuanced feature distinctions, which can be leveraged to identify objects based on inferred attributes.  In addition, the approach includes a novel procedure for inferring attribute representations from datasets assuming objects' geometric symmetry.  The algorithm's performance was tested on three datasets and compared to other methods, revealing improved accuracy and computational efficiency.

We've analyzed the data from a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, based on our comprehensive photometry observations taken over 318 days. These observations revealed detailed insights into the binary's behavior and allowed us to refine the time of the mid-eclipse. Using individual filter light curve fittings, we determined the low-mass star components and companion star sizes of the binary, finding the white dwarf has a radius of 0.031 R sun, while its companion has a radius of 0.013 R sun at an angle of 87.7 degrees. Furthermore, based on our most suitable model, we estimated the secondary star temperature to be around 5200 K with an error margin of 100 K. Notably, though the system's overall orbit period remains stable at 211.88283 days, it exhibits slight irregularities in its progress. Nonetheless, our research suggests the binary's behavior can be predicted with great accuracy using a simplified model.

In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the distances between points in the feature space to vary, the number of transport ships, and the costs associated with transporting, the choice of global pooling method is effectively determined by just three factors. This reveals the underlying logic behind the performance of existing global pooling methods and provides a pathway for the creation of new, high-performance global poolings through the modification of the distance function. To this end, a new global averaging pooling (GAP) has been developed, which outperforms current global pooling methods, including learned and unlearned instances, as evidenced by our experiments on image classification and segmentation tasks.

The primary objective of this research is to examine AGN classification using the $g$-derived emission line diagnostic. We analyzed 1,624 Sloan Digital Sky Survey spectra with a type I Seyfert nucleus, identifying 94% as elliptical or spiral galaxies. Unbiased samples of elliptical and spiral galaxies with type I Seyfert nuclei have distinct characteristics. Spiral galaxies display stronger high-ionization line emissions and are more likely to be associated with larger galaxy velocities. The presence of elliptical galaxies with type I Seyfert nuclei suggests AGN are likely to be found in all galaxy types, particularly those that are massively star-forming. Additionally, further classification using the $g$-derived diagnostic revealed type I Seyfert nuclei exhibit both neutral/emission characteristics, suggesting that the line of sight to the nucleus often includes star-forming regions. However, type II AGN, obtained from the same spectra, generally indicate that the line of sight to the nucleus is primarily obstructed by star-forming regions.

This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of general rotational surfaces in the 4-dimensional Euclidean space, focusing on the cases of planar and non-planar, flat and twisted types. Key aspects addressed include establishing a new parametric representation, determining the second order approximate distance, calculating the Gaussian curvature, and classifying these surfaces based on their type. Specifically, the research reveals that a Clifford torus can be regarded as a non-planar, flat general rotation surface.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Consequently, we carried out an exhaustive analysis, comparing several deep
unroll-based methods for generating depth maps on two diverse datasets. Our
results indicate that a straightforward yet efficient model is sufficient for
deriving meaningful depth estimates from untagged videos. Importantly, we found
that refining this estimate through supervision brings significant benefits.
Finally, we established that while our approach does not surpass the performance
of the widely-used image-based pre-training on the fine-tuning stage, it does
improve it, leading us to conclude that deep pre-training for semantic
segmentation through depth estimation is feasible and potentially more effective
in certain contexts.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the diversity and coherence of generated stories by up to 23.4% and 30.9%, respectively, over a leading non-neural time-series narration method. Furthermore, we show that TCube excels at enhancing coherence by up to 229.9% and diversity by up to 46.4% when compared to a leading neural story generation model that draws inspiration from SOTA neural time-series models.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

This study explores the well-posedness of global solutions, dependence on initial data, and potential loss of regularity in strictly hyperbolic equations with certain properties. These equations feature coefficients that experience moderate blow-up as sublogarithmic growth, represented by the function $|\ln t|^\gamma$ where $0 < \gamma < 1$. By applying a specific metric on the phase space, we can categorize these equations and examine their coefficients, which have polynomial bounds in x, x-derivatives, and a specific rate of decrease in t. We leverage a Planck function, based on this metric, to split the phase space and define relevant generalized symbol classes. Through the use of a conjugating pseudodifferential operator, which we term the loss operator, we establish an energy estimate and identify a link between the loss of regularity and the phase space metric and singular behavior. Our analysis shows that the solution undergoes a small, yet arbitrary, loss relative to its initial datum in a Sobolev space adapted to the loss operator.

This paper offers a summary of recent developments in Japanese word segmentation techniques, specifically focusing on new data sets and segmentation methods not covered in our prior overview on Chinese word segmentation. Due to differences between Japanese and Chinese, there are unique obstacles to segmentation, such as less rigid sentence structures and compound words with varying parts. Recent research has yielded multiple Japanese word segmentation models, including those inspired by Chinese and utilizing distributed representations. Unlike Chinese, these models often employ more complex architectures, yet less attention has been given to developing new data sets for Japanese word segmentation. In response, this paper introduces the Japanese Berkeley parser bank, an annotated corpus of texts classified into eight categories. Additionally, this corpus addresses the lack of data by offering a new training set, called Japanese Word Segmentation Bank.

On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This leads to observations such as users contributing identical knowledge across multiple posts, users reusing links for promotional purposes, and the issue of links referencing overwhelming amounts of data that can make information retrieval difficult. Our findings offer actionable insights to Stack Overflow moderators and researchers, including the recommendation to implement a centralized knowledge management system for maintaining and updating shared resources to preserve the integrity of the community's collaborative knowledge base.

Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with and without baryonic feedback. Contrary to standard CDM, SIDM can form isothermal cores, and its effectiveness isn't largely influenced by long-term baryonic feedback processes. Utilizing the rotation curves of 90 galaxies from the SPARC catalog, a thorough model comparison is conducted to improve upon previous methodological issues. Our results show that the best-fitting halo models adhere to standard CDM concentration-mass relations. Although SIDM and feedback-influenced CDM outperform the non-feedback CDM in accounting for rotation curves of galaxies with varying surface brightnesses, neither model has a strong statistical advantage when compared to each other in explaining galaxy diversity in the given sample.

Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of an up-to-date climate knowledge base, we have built one by curating existing knowledge sources
and integrating them with new information from peer-reviewed studies. Additionally, we have revised
a popular climate knowledge base with the aim of reducing misinformation. To guide knowledge acquisition,
we have developed knowledge questions, criteria for determining valuable knowledge entries.
A comprehensive evaluation of our climate knowledge base through human assessors revealed significantly higher accuracy
compared to two popular automated evaluation methods. Furthermore, our climate knowledge base now enables the integration
of new machine learning-based techniques to score the effectiveness of existing climate information.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive strategy for extracting symptoms by temporarily removing commonly mentioned symptoms from the original data source.
Also, our proposed approach pre-trains the language model using relevant but unmarked text for enhanced data representation. 
Experimental results on multiple symptom types from three distinct data sources reveal that incorporating these strategies significantly enhances symptom extraction accuracy.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, given its relevance due to autonomous driving's inherent complexities and environmental dependencies. In particular, autonomous driving poses significant challenges as a supervised learning problem due to dynamic interactions with pedestrians, vehicles, and road conditions. In view of the relative novelty of the area of study, this work aims to provide an introductory overview of the underlying theory and core concepts of deep reinforcement learning, accompanied by the implementation details of our developed framework. A series of simulation-based evaluations using PyTLD demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed model.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural network architectures. We also outline a thorough training protocol for RNNs and conduct initial experiments to validate our approach, demonstrating that RNNs can reach performance comparable to standard neural networks while ensuring they can be successfully evaluated on existing hardware that mimics bio-realistic neural systems, such as the Salus neuromorphic board.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like video encoding and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe.

A computational method for resolving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is presented, using an approximating function derived from the eigenvalues of a modified eigenproblem equation.  By utilizing a variable sampling process that focuses data collection on the areas most critical to solution resolution, this algorithm efficiently distributes resources. It then employs the collected information to produce approximations for the sought-after eigenvalues and eigenvectors through further processing. Several numerical demonstrations highlight the performance of this solution strategy.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new results and proofs in various contexts.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry down to $SO(N_{F})$. Our findings derive from an ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric theory, specifically with anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking.

Machine learning models such as random forests and AdaBoost have proven effective across many fields but their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their predictions. Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a new approach, Disentangled Attribution Curves, has been developed to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through simple and easy-to-interpret curves. DAC provides users with the opportunity to gain insights into the models in much the same way as they can with linear models. Furthermore, it enables users to make adjustments to characteristics and observe the expected change in the model's output. In addition to its practical uses, DAC also facilitates the identification of disentangled variables - variables whose effects on the model cannot be replaced by combinations of other variables. In order to demonstrate its effectiveness, DAC has been tested on data from real-world fields such as politics and finance as well as from fields such as sports analytics and fantasy sports.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data.  Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation.  Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application.  This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and system information, introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication time, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation.

The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was validated through various test protocols.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering rules in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically generate system call filters in real-time according to an application's execution pattern, previously unknown system calls can be quickly accommodated without requiring human intervention. Unlike static analysis-based techniques, Timeloops dynamically creates filters on a per-container basis and adapts to changing system calls in runtime. Timeloops' implementation is now available online at: https://github.com/blanklys/Timeloops.

Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models are capable of accurately representing all linear classifiers.
Consequently, these models can be trained to achieve perfect accuracy on linear separation tasks within complex product space structures composed of multiple geometric environments.
This capability enables the representation of linear classifiers in compact, high-quality forms within complex geometric environments, ultimately contributing to more effective data representation and classification applications.

This introduction focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control methods that account for uncertainty in constraints, illustrated through a linear system under unpredictable conditions. The corresponding Matlab code is also accessible online for reference purposes.

This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the data enable the efficient reduction of processing requirements during the learning process. Our findings demonstrate the potential for significant data-dependent savings in computational cost, potentially leading to substantial performance gains.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the dominance of one species or coexistence of both species under specific conditions of noise and dispersal. The model shows that increasing noise can have different effects, leading to the stabilization of both single-species and two-species states. The transition from a single-species state to a two-species state is characterized by a supercritical Hopf bifurcation based on the mean dispersal distance. The model's findings demonstrate that increased noise can facilitate the coexistence of species in ecological models.
We prove that von Neumann algebras associated with compact regions within abelian quantum double models have infinite type $II$.

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a coherent feedback loop. Furthermore, our findings confirm that both the steady and dynamic states of this system exhibit genuine tripartite entanglement. We utilize the logarithmic negativity to quantify quantum correlations between individual subsystems, as well as genuine tripartite entanglement through a nonzero minimum residual contangle. We investigate experimentally feasible parameters that enable the generation of tripartite entanglement and demonstrate its significant enhancement with coherent feedback by adjusting the beam splitter's reflective parameter. Additionally, the proposed entanglement exhibits robustness against thermal effects, making our approach a valuable asset for applications in quantum information processing.

We've obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qgg$, $g \to gq\bar{q}$ and $g \to ggg$. The exact expressions are derived within dimensionless QCD and include the results of a specific integral up to its second-order expansion. Additionally, we've evaluated the associated splitting functions. Our results are crucial and necessary for creating subtraction and integrated-subtraction terms in next-to-next-to-next-to leading order cross-section computations.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to investigate sundials in Indonesia.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we have developed an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of this algorithm.

This study introduces a cutting-edge technique for comprehensive signal processing of pulsed laser data collected during two-dimensional vibrometry tests. Our advanced signal processing methods enhance data analysis by accurately capturing and displaying sample responses, spectral information, and phase data for complex samples. The technique utilizes a distributed acquisition approach to break down large data sets into manageable sections, which are then analyzed via the Fast Fourier Transform to extract essential frequency and phase data. Our results demonstrate excellent agreement with conventional time-domain techniques, showcasing the technique's effectiveness in detecting subtle changes, identifying sample-specific features, and determining the phase shift between samples. The proposed technique boasts a remarkable capacity for high dynamic range distributed FFT analysis, outperforming other techniques in terms of processing speed. Our research aims to expand the applications of two-dimensional vibrometry, enabling the detection of non-measurable samples, and offering novel insights into sample responses, spectral information, and phase transitions.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and only one binary relation are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and relations, whose models consist of undirected graphs, thereby providing a spectrum of possible cardinalities. Furthermore, we prove that the spectrum of $\Phi'$ is both exhaustive and expansive over the spectrum of the original sentence $\Phi$.  Consequently, for any non-atomic sentence $\Phi$ with a finite model having a specific cardinality, there is also a sentence $\Phi'$ with an even more extensive spectrum.  Additionally, we note that the original sentence $\Phi$ may have a model of any desired finite cardinality, leading to a sentence $\Phi'$ with a model of exactly the same size.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study derives a straightforward, combinatorial method for determining the general formula for calculating the potential positions of an $n$-step random walk in a $d$-dimensional space. The derivation employs two crucial concepts: multi-set combinations and recursive function relationships, which ultimately lead to the identification of a specific number of potential positions. The study also examines the asymptotic number of positions for extensive $n$, considering both exact and approximate scenarios.

This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We explored how in the GOP model the spacelike transition surface at the classical singularity replaces it. Utilizing transformations in the coordinates, the authors were able to extend the metric to the white hole region, which led to discovering that the structure of the quantum black hole bears resemblance to that of wormholes, with their radii at the throat equal to each other. Moreover, the authors found that not only is the throat where the curvature is concentrated but also that the curvature becomes concentrated as one approaches the throat. After verifying that the throat is stable under linearized perturbations, the authors then investigated the quasinormal frequencies of quantum black holes. For scalar field perturbations, the authors were able to derive the quantum analogs of the established s and p quasinormal frequencies of Kerr black holes, and further research revealed that these quantum frequencies are similar to those of wormholes. The quantum corrections were found to decrease the frequency of antipodal modes and increase it for proximal modes. For gravitational perturbations, the quantum analogs of the Regge-Wheeler spherically symmetric modes were explored, and it was discovered that quantum effects lower the frequency of antipodal modes and increase the frequency of proximal modes. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. Conversely, employing generative models can mitigate these drawbacks, though they introduce an increased computational requirement. Our analysis specifically examines the capability of generative models, particularly Variational Auto-Encoders, in enhancing the effectiveness of MitM attacks on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. Our findings show that existing deep learning models are susceptible to MitM attacks; however, generative models can improve the success rate of these attacks, though at the expense of doubled computational processing. Our research offers the first investigation into MitM attacks on DNN models and existing data sets, with a particular focus on the potential of generative models.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions. It differs from earlier studies which focused solely on dark matter creation accompanied by a top quark pair by also investigating cases where a top quark was present individually. Multiple criteria for selecting data categories that correspond to either a top quark or a top quark pair were developed to determine the outcomes of this study. Those categories included instances where a top quark or pair had low energy and where a top quark was absent, which corresponded to 92% of all such occurrences. Furthermore, it was discovered that the rates of occurrence of dark matter and a top quark or pair of quarks slightly exceeded the predicted rates of occurrence. Masses between 0.25 TeV and 1.1 TeV for a scalar or pseudoscalar mediator and between 0.25 TeV and 1.4 TeV for a vector mediator were constrained. Lastly, the results of this study were in line with the standard model predictions for instances where a top quark was present, but not for instances where a top quark was absent.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ranked preference data, we analyze the testable implications of the key assumptions underpinning their identification argument. This analysis also offers a novel assessment of the biases resulting from these assumption violations. Ultimately, these findings empower researchers to evaluate the reliability of these assumptions and determine the practical impact of their breaches. Utilizing the identified method, we investigate the post-secondary field of study return on investment in Norway and Denmark, exploring potential cross-country differences. Our results indicate significant correlation between fields of study return on investment in both countries, particularly after eliminating fields where identification assumption breaches occur.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles.
As a result, a huge number of $J/\psi$ decays occur annually, creating opportunities for accurate measurements of various transition rates and decay processes involving the creation of antineutrons, hyperons and their counterparts.
This review aims to summarize findings from existing studies, discuss their precision and recent developments, in addition to highlighting promising areas for investigation and potential improvements using cutting-edge research tools.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in a significant potential difference between the mass of the smaller binary and the third body.  Recent studies have suggested that in hierarchical triples, the differential accretion phenomenon is unlikely to occur when the mass of the smaller binary is greater than two-thirds that of the third body.  Utilizing numerical simulations, the current research validated a theoretical model for calculating the boundary of differential accretion in hierarchical triples, depending on the initial mass ratio of the smaller binary to the third body.  The study discovered that in hierarchical triples, the boundary of differential accretion is located at a mass ratio of 0.64, with the mass ratio being defined as the mass of the smaller binary relative to the third body.  The study also found that in hierarchical triples, the accretion mass ratio can fluctuate widely, often exceeding 0.9, a value similar to that of binary systems.  The research identified several factors that can influence the accretion mass ratio, including the mass ratio of the smaller binary to the third body and the mass fraction of the third body that is added to the less massive star. This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, highlighting the spacetimes' ability to accurately capture the universe's intrinsic structure on a cosmological scale.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the benefits of both image restoration and image segmentation frameworks. The integration of image restoration techniques such as denoising, deblurring, and demosaicking proves particularly effective in addressing issues like incomplete and imperfect labels. Our model architecture includes an image restoration stage followed by an image segmentation stage, treating the output of the former as input. This design can be applied to both complete and partial segmentation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the model's capability to improve segmentation performance when given noise-corrupted images and improve robustness to partial labels when provided with clean images. This model also offers enhanced feature learning, particularly useful for segmentation tasks. Our method was tested on various segmentation tasks, including the benchmark SIFT dataset and medical image segmentation with the BRATS dataset.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research provides constraints on ultra-light boson properties, inferring that their masses would need to be significantly lower than what is currently allowed, at a much higher order of magnitude.

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this issue, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Brian simulator and seamlessly integrating with existing workflows. This emulator successfully emulated the processing elements and plasticity mechanisms of spiking neural networks on IBM's TrueNorth chip, across various programming interfaces. Furthermore, our implementation ensured that the computational elements of the chip were accurately simulated, enabling the emulation of more than a million neurons and 255 true north chips on a standard, 16-GB laptop. Additionally, our emulator allowed for the precise replication of synapse efficiency and efficiency for each neuron, thus accurately simulating synapse plasticity during emulation. This emulator has been used in various areas, such as validating the emulated chip's original specification, validating variations of the chip's original specification, investigating wireless communication on the chip, and comparing different learning rule implementations.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies a new aspect of these storm sources associated with minor solar flares. It reveals the existence of two distinct modes of co-evolution: a "sausage-like" mode, in which storm intensity decreases while size increases, and a "torsional" mode, in which storm size changes correlate with sky-orientation changes. The researchers have also observed, for the first time in this context, the transition of these storm sources from the "torsional" mode to the "saussian-like" mode, facilitated by a flare. These findings support the theory of increased magnetic stress in complex active region structures that later collapse into instability, producing flares and significant changes in particle acceleration and/or interaction with neighboring regions. The discovery of the "torsional" mode suggests that recently-discovered "quiet sun" storm sources may have a different origin, associated with minor solar flares.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated laser system to capture a small cloud of $^{87}$Rb atoms. This novel MOT setup eliminates the need for a separate laser source, offering streamlined integration with other atomic or molecular trapping techniques.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, such as radial free fall, Bondi accretion, and Anderson's rotating accretion, to determine mass accretion rates. Specifically, we consider how angular momentum influences the process, particularly in models of rotating accretication, for which derived solutions are compared against those established boundary conditions.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters, or if they can also be found in less crowded environments. The discovery of AZaurus, a rich field containing six massive stars and seven possible candidate O stars, presents significant implications for this question. By examining the cluster's properties and comparing them to theoretical models, it's found that AZaurus has a mass greater than what's typically observed for massive star-forming regions, but its mass distribution doesn't follow the predicted universal law for star clusters. Instead, it's thought that AZaurus could be a unique example of a massive star embedded in a less crowded environment due to the absence of clear-density boundaries, or it could be a fragment of a larger cluster disrupted by interactions with the galactic disk. Regardless of its history, the presence of massive stars outside of dense clusters complicates theoretical efforts to explain the origins and dispersal of these stars.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO competition challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and achieving improved results in L1 distance and comparable results in L2 distance to the original images, while also qualitatively evaluating the generated colors.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. Conversely, issues with overfitting may arise in scenarios where the matrix determinant approaches zero. To mitigate such cases, we've introduced an enhanced version of the method that incorporates L1, L2, and cross-validation techniques. Furthermore, our numerical analysis indicates that the computational cost of our scheme scales linearly with the dataset size, making it significantly more efficient than standard ANN training methods, which have a quadratic time complexity.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with several significant initiatives during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory but have yet to observe them in practice.
This study demonstrates the successful detection of line waves in a real-world setting, achieved by characterizing the line waves produced by two custom-designed metasurfaces.
Each metasurface consists of a periodic arrangement of gold strips on top of a substrate, but with the structure modified to account for symmetry.
The line waves were excited and measured through a simple setup, and the results confirmed that the detected signal aligns with theoretical predictions.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable cognitive systems for one-shot learning across diverse robots and tasks. 

It's difficult for robots to achieve prolonged autonomy due to limitations in current multi-agent LfD techniques, such as communication issues, perception challenges, and reasoning dilemmas. To tackle these problems, a new architecture called DREAM is proposed, which incorporates a new communication protocol inspired by human dialogue, a perception module using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNN), and a reasoning engine employing Graph Neural Networks (GNN). 

To validate DREAM, the approach is applied in a new dataset called DREAM, which features complex macro tasks performed by two robots in different environments. Experimental results demonstrate that DREAM achieves superior one-shot learning capabilities with an accuracy rate of 87.14%, substantially outperforming existing multi-agent LfD techniques such as COMA by 33.33%.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves proving the asymptotic bias of a particular estimator.  To validate the method's validity, an alternative approach has been designed.  Establishing the validity involves proving the consistency of a specific estimator.  To broaden the method's application, a specific adaptation has been implemented.  Establishing the effectiveness of the modified method involves proving a consistency result.  Several simulations have been conducted to evaluate the performance of the new estimator.  To further assess the method, a specific criterion has been used.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by training a relation extraction
model and then applying it to the knowledge graph link prediction task, achieving
results exceeding current state-of-the-art benchmarks, notably obtaining 81.7%
on the TAC-KBP dataset and 73.56% on the SemEval2014 task datasets.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of anisotropy, temperature, and baryonic chemical potential. By obtaining the Schrödinger equation solution in a closed form, binding energies of quarkonium states have been calculated, and their dependence on anisotropy, temperature, and chemical potential has been analyzed. Interestingly, anisotropy was found to decrease the dissociation temperature of quarkonia, while chemical potential was found to have a minimal effect compared to temperature. Moreover, the study reveals the anisotropy-temperature relationship and the anisotropy-chemical potential relationship, and it also demonstrates the N-dimensional nature of the binding energy of quarkonium states, which exhibits a decrease with increasing N.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being magnetic and others not. As this material was cooled down, its magnetic chains initially aligned equally in both directions below a 15 K critical point, but exhibited independent alignments at lower temperatures. In Nd3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms formed a two-dimensional pattern, with all magnetic domains aligning equally in all directions below a 17 K critical point. Our findings indicate that the dependence on temperature for the magnetic arrangements of the ruthenium atoms in both compounds is highly similar, yet their magnetic domain patterns differ significantly.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative dual-
MLP approach that applies distinct periodic activations to different signal
components, enabling a significant boost in generalization. This method
facilitates the efficient representation of multiple signals, such as
colorful images and moving videos, by incorporating a second MLP with
periodic activations. In our experiments, this approach leads to improved
results on image and video representation tasks and paves the way for
future applications in processing multiple signals.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift within semi-supervised learning where labelled data constitute a source domain, and unlabelled data serve as a target domain. Employing domain-invariant representations alone doesn't account for the labelled target data. To address this limitation, we combine adaptation with semi-supervised learning, training a model in a manner that ensures its representations remain consistent across domains and that predictions made on the labelled source data match those made on the unlabelled target data. This approach yields superior results on synthetic and real-world tasks compared to disparate adaptation of either importance weights or features.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, incorporating 'augmented' variables, known as XAUG variables, alongside standard input, then applies a layer-by-layer relevance analysis to both types of networks. XAUG variables are merged with intermediate network layers and utilised in final stages to interpret the classification outcome. Analysis shows XAUG variables enhance discrimination capabilities when combined with low-level features, in some instances capturing the classification entirely. This method, combined with the relevance analysis, allows researchers to determine crucial information networks rely on. In the study's findings, XAUG variables identified key features in tagged jets that differentiate them from untagged jets. By merging these with LHC data, researchers could reconstruct the full shower structure of a tagged jet, significantly reducing uncertainty. This method holds potential for both training networks to increase performance and extracting valuable insights into particle physics.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical framework was then applied to calculate and compute symbols representing optical response properties. This was achieved by manually defining the action of each layer group on electric currents and determining the relevant little group for each irreducible domain. The computed symbols were then summed over all domains to obtain the full layer group action. The study confirmed that the second double cover, often denoted as $2\widetilde{g}$, is relevant in the analysis of optical properties.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/R, where R represents the sphere's curvature radius, yielding countable energy and momentum spectrums for freely moving particles. A theoretical maximum for possible momenta in S^3 corresponds to its diameter, the de Broglie wavelength λ_R = πR. Building on this, the definitions and relationships for covariant position operators in terms of geodesic normal coordinates, along with commutator relations for position and momentum, are developed.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, we investigate the dynamics of two scalar fields, 
where one is a fundamental complex field and the other a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone 
boson arising from a U(1) symmetry breaking in the infrared. The interaction 
between these fields is analyzed in detail, particularly how it influences the 
global symmetry structure, which complements a simple gauge sector consisting of 
a fundamental gauge boson and associated fermions. The model's symmetry and 
symmetries of the dual effective Lagrangian are thoroughly examined, along with 
the mass spectrum of the observed particles. The outcome indicates the feasibility 
of a feasible infrared fixed point for the coupling of the fundamental complex field 
and the related global symmetry structure, which could potentially be linked to the 
mass of the fundamental scalar in the standard model.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements and sensations to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's kinetic energy ratio to its gravitational energy. This alteration led to increased binary mass and enabled a more precise determination of how a system's mass is generated. Furthermore, researchers created a diagram to represent binary system formation based on total core mass and kinetic energy ratio. This study also recorded and presented various properties of proto-stellar fragments, including formation mass, thermal to gravitational energy ratio, and kinetic energy ratio.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable kernel, utilising an alternative parameter modification to enhance its performance. Furthermore, it incorporates an optimal kernel choice method, facilitating a comparison with other methods of feature extraction and ICA. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated on simulated data sets, real data sets, and binary image classification tasks, demonstrating improved results compared to existing methods. The research further examines the computational efficiency of the approach by analyzing its processing time, enabling kernel replication for ongoing research projects without compromising performance. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach offers enhanced feature extraction and ICA capabilities, along with an easily replicable code and optimal kernel selection.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems.
