Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new model, called the dynamical binary neural network (D2NN), has been developed for sequence learning purposes. This model extends the traditional McNulty model and incorporates asymmetrical connections between binary neurons for sequence memorization and generation. Furthermore, it demonstrates the equivalence of supervisory sequence learning algorithms to optimization problems involving the minimization of a difference measure between token distributions in phase space. This model also facilitates the effective learning of binary sequences and their reverse versions, in addition to allowing the learning of homographic binary sequences. However, our investigation has revealed limitations to supervisory learning for certain heterographic sequences. Consequently, a post-training pruning process has been devised to eliminate dependencies on undesirable neural connections. This new model is anticipated to offer a viable alternative to existing neural network models for sequence learning tasks.

This study addresses the issue of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model limitations
when confronted with novel scene text examples during training, leading to reduced
performance in recognizing unseen text. To overcome this challenge, we introduce
the concept of a semantic embedding space for scene text features. By utilizing
contrastive learning to create a unified understanding of text semantics within this
space, we enable current state-of-the-art OCR models to achieve superior performance
on previously unseen text instances. The proposed approach is evaluated on the
Standard-Timer and Arabic-Timer datasets and demonstrates a significant 6.48% and
3.38% improvement in word accuracy for the English and Arabic languages, respectively.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems. This framework is then applied to a famous model for phase transitions, allowing for the identification of random equilibrium states and precise validation of critical points.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This research proposes Multivariate Functional Principal Component Regression (MFPCR) to address these challenges. MFPCR is an advanced method that combines principles of functional data analysis and multivariate statistics. It enhances the performance of traditional Principal Component Regression (PCR) by effectively handling high-dimensional data in an industrial setting. Further research could involve exploring the performance of MFPCR under different sample availability scenarios.

We have created a detailed analysis of the remnants of two disrupted galaxies that are now part of the Milky Way. By using modeling the galaxies' orbits and how they dissolved, we identified key time periods in their disruption. For the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus galaxy, we found that most of its material arrived at the galaxies' center approximately 8 to 10 billion years ago, with its star-forming core forming around 8 billion years ago and lasting for about 2 billion years. Conversely, the Wukong/LMS-1 galaxy is thought to have dissolved more quickly than the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus galaxy. Our findings also suggested that a massive black hole may have influenced the galaxies' centers, with evidence of a 100 million solar mass black hole potentially remaining in the galaxies' center. With further research involving more precise stellar ages, we look forward to refining our understanding of these galaxies' orbits and ages.

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the graded profinite \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}[[G]]-module \pi_*(X). This is demonstrated with an equivalence for certain conditions on G and Z: specifically, (Z[[G]])_{hG} is shown to be equivalent to Z in those scenarios, with supplementary methods for further investigation provided.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnetic moment is relatively weak.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on improving the training efficiency itself. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, for the first time, addresses this gap by optimizing the training process of CNNs. By incorporating a module that mimics the structure of a click-through rate prediction system, ClickTrain allows for pruning during training. Unlike existing methods, ClickTrain does not require an additional inference pruning step. Moreover, ClickTrain employs a soft pruning approach that retains the original network, thus facilitating easy deployment after pruning for potential accuracy enhancements. Our experiments demonstrate that ClickTrain outperforms existing methods, including a notable 40% reduction in training time, and achieves significant gains in computational cost for model pruning, with a 6.3x reduction in overhead, while maintaining nearly the same accuracy for inference.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific structural rule. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 (a K-type star located about 450 light years from Earth) in a 75-day period. Using the TESS satellite, the planet was initially detected in 2020, but it wasn't confirmed until a follow-up study using various ground-based telescopes, which also found that another planet, TOI-5542.02, exists in a 5.5-day orbit. Both planets are believed to be gas giants due to their size relative to their host star. Research suggests that TOI-5542.01 could be a young and massive planet given its significant transiting probability of 81%, whereas TOI-5542.02 has a lower transiting probability of 32%. By further analyzing the data, it was found that TOI-5542.01 exhibits unusual behavior, such as uneven surface temperature distribution, and possibly out-of-equilibrium atmospheric composition. Moreover, patterns indicate that the planet might be in a dynamic state of equilibrium. By comparing the orbital characteristics of the two planets, it was observed that there is no indication of gravitational interaction. By studying the host star, which is relatively metal-rich (based on its specific location on the M$_\mathrm{g}$-Fe/H diagram), it was discovered that TOI-5542.01 follows a trend of giant planets being more common around metal-rich hosts. The research

Sequential decision-making operations management issues, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Researchers have developed two main methods for solving CMDPs: sampling-based and convex methods. Although the sampling-based approach can handle large systems with high dimensions, it may face issues with sample efficiency and state action coverage. On the other hand, the convex approach ensures optimal solutions but often becomes infeasible for large systems due to non-convexity. To resolve these limitations, a new approach is proposed, combining the benefits of both methods by using a sampling-based approach for large systems and converting the resulting point estimates into a convex optimization problem. The approach also addresses the issue of sparse systems, reducing the number of states and actions necessary for solving the CMDP by identifying a minimal set of influential systems. The resulting point estimates are then used to develop an approximate value function and an optimal policy. The approach is evaluated on a data-driven inventory management problem, demonstrating the efficacy of this method for large systems and the effectiveness of the state action coverage algorithm for managing data noise.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective classifier capable of recognizing such a wide range of symbols must be developed. Initially, this study addressed the challenge of segmentation by applying the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering method. Results showed a 90% success rate for segmenting complex mathematical expressions and a 90% success rate for segmenting basic mathematical expressions. Then, this research focused on recognizing mathematical symbols in both horizontal and vertical orientations, achieving a 90% accuracy rate in total, after testing with 300 different mathematical symbols.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone. The BPS states of the theory correspond to specific cohomology classes on the cone, and these classes can be calculated using a twisted Dolbeault complex on the cone. The process of quantization can be applied to an orbifolded hyper-Kahler cone. The paper focuses on an example of a hyper-Kahler cone based on a two-dimensional $N= (4|4)$ superconformal boundary change. The BPS states of the theory are equivalent to classes in a specific twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the cone. The cohomology is determined by a combinatorial rule. The paper examines BPS state counts for the theory, and these counts match the homology of a certain complex on the dual of the cone's Lie bialgebra. The complex is formed by connecting Lie derivatives of the Dolbeault classes, where the connections are specified by an invariant on the dual of the cone's Lie bialgebra.

We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures tends to spread information more efficiently and result in higher final infection rates. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the impact of network topology on disease propagation can outweigh the effects of temperature and interaction types.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning methods are commonly used for solving complex decision-making problems. However, they often struggle with getting stuck in suboptimal local minima due to the choice of stochastic gradient descent for parameter updates. In contrast, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a hybrid of Hamming network and HMC, has shown potential in exploring the posterior distribution more efficiently. By integrating HMC into actor-critic learning, KHMC has demonstrated improved performance in exploring the action space and achieved higher reward rates. Building upon this concept, researchers proposed Hamming-out (HHMC), a variant of KHMC, in order to further increase its novel aspects. HHMC has proven to be more efficient than current best methods in a range of tested environments and has significantly reduced training time from what was previously required to achieve similar results.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result of our investigation, we propose a novel, refined criterion for identifying potential $\textbf{twin-prime candidates}$. Our analysis indicates that the new criterion not only enhances the search process but also makes it more efficient by reducing the number of candidates to a subset of those produced by the previous method. We then demonstrate the potential utility of this refined criterion by applying it to identify new, high-range twin-prime pairs. We have run a test using this approach as far out as $p$ values approaching $10^{10}$, but due to computational constraints, our search has reached only a $p$ value of $10^{8}$ in the upper range. Consequently, we were able to find five $\textbf{Twin Prime Challenge of the Century}$ candidates ($p$ values of $1003579681$, $2399396873$, $4190773777$, $4432579453$, and $4766986757$), but regretfully, we did not identify any novel twin-prime pairs during this test.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller, to achieve time-domain control of the robot's movement. Experimental results from both simulated and real-world tests confirm the efficacy of this approach. A key advantage of this method is its adaptability for use with any type of sensor, provided it has a known output that can be manipulated to achieve target navigation goals.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral data, combining these with information on its temperature and the sub-millimeter spectrum of the Neptune system. By accounting for the reflectance from an icy surface featuring chlorethane and other icy components, along with a time- and frequency-averaged radiative model of the Neptune system, we resolve the discrepancy in the visible and sub-millimeter spectrum. This reveals the presence of multiple spectral features in Nereid's spectrum that cannot be explained by standard models, indicating the possibility that similar objects could be composed of bodies with neutral-sloped spectra.

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T_n(q)$, we find $(q+1)^{(n-1)}q^{\frac{3(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}$ affine planes of order $q$, where points and lines within these planes satisfy specific submodule properties. These affine planes are ultimately shown to be extendable to a projective plane of order $q$, where free cyclic submodules corresponding to non-unimodular images of rank $n-1$ are present.

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that key properties of models can be captured through infinitary universal sequences over specific notions of forcing, thereby establishing significant model-theoretic inequalities. This method can also be applied to investigate relationships between key set-theoretic characteristics, thereby providing new insights into their possible values and ranges.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism tuning is eliminated. Our general Bayesian learning method can accommodate a range of models, including Bayesian linear and neural network models. Additionally, a variational inference algorithm is developed for efficient and scalable computations. The theoretical soundness of our approach is confirmed through established guarantees, which, along with simulations and real-world data tests, show our solution's superior performance compared to current offline data solutions.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-body excitations are governed by an effective single-particle Hamiltonian based on the non-interacting wave functions of the system. Furthermore, we found a zero-energy excitation characteristic to these bound states with dispersion determined by the minimal quantum metric. Using the framework of topological quantum chemistry, we categorize the bound state spectrum, leading to the identification of Cooper pairs exhibiting Weyl nodes, high angular momentum pairing, and fragile topological features. Our analysis also demonstrates that electron kinetic energy as a perturbation maximizes pairing strength at half filling, similar to the phenomenon observed in twisted bilayer graphene.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids distribution as the limit of a specific mathematical structure and demonstrate that it is characterized by a specific set of mathematical structures.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods can often be independently supported or identified through statistical tests. However, due to the complexity of joint probability models, determining whether a given cluster is significantly distinct often proves challenging. We propose a novel approach to address this issue by using continuous data methods in a spatial autologistic model framework. This model formulates the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances as a dependent variable and species presence/absence as independent variables. By treating species presence/absence as linear components, this model allows for the exploration of non-linear species interactions and provides a statistical tool for assessing the significance of clusters through spatial autocorrelation analysis. The proposed method is supported by an example analysis of bat species in a region of Queensland, Australia.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. To address this issue and improve efficiency, we propose an integrated framework that can effectively handle both RGB and RGB-D images using a unified architecture. This framework extracts image features from RGB inputs and context features from RGB-D inputs (or a compressed representation thereof), combining them through a cross-attention mechanism to produce salient object maps. By incorporating context information, our method outperforms existing approaches on various datasets, demonstrating improved accuracy and computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on salient object detection tasks.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Additionally, we prove that this problem can be transformed into an equivalent form, which enables us to identify a specific range, -2^n < N < 2^(-n+1), in which all possible values of N can be generated from a structured set.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. To address these issues, we present a novel mathematical framework that accounts for these two distinct forms of noise in CT imaging. This method yields the unique minimum-norm solution for the reconstructed image, which surpasses other methods, such as the standard filtered back projection, as well as more recent techniques like penalized-likelihood solutions and the recently-proposed minimum-norm penalized-likelihood solution in terms of its stability and accuracy.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) in resource-constrained environments is a complex challenge, particularly when dealing with historical documents. One significant obstacle is the presence of novel characters, known as Novelty, which hinders model performance. Existing methods for Novelty handling are often incompatible with resource scarcity settings. To address this issue, we present a novel approach called Novelty Node, integrated within a Sequential Neural Network, to overcome Novelty during HTR in low resource settings. The method was evaluated using the RAISE-BT19 dataset and demonstrated superior results compared to baseline models.

We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements to much higher energies ($\sim$80 MeV) than previously achieved. Our method enables us to derive a more comprehensive three-nucleon interaction matrix that can be applied in a wider energy range. We utilized our storage approach to calculate all distinct three-nucleon interaction matrix elements within the $E_{\text{max}}$=8 channel, and our findings show good agreement with more rigorous calculations. Our study demonstrates that a truncated 3N interaction can be sufficient for conducting microscopically informed calculations of atomic nuclei.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function to describe all graviton supermultiplet amplitudes of any rank at two-loop order. The study also provides an approach for deriving two-loop amplitude formulas for higher rank components through preamplitude construction and reveals that the general four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals encode the full two-loop logarithmic discontinuities of all AdS$_5$ superamplitudes.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices is typically characterized by using extensive data parallelism where various operations are executed simultaneously on numerous data elements.  Nevertheless, the rising demand for simulating complex real-world phenomena through Multiple-Objects High Performance Computing (MOHPC) has brought about a new challenge: processing and managing a considerable number of objects while ensuring that simultaneous operations do not undermine the reliability of the results.  In response, the concept of Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) was introduced where a single method is applied to multiple objects, thereby allowing for independent processing.  In this research, we introduce four novel approaches to determine the optimal object partitioning that maximizes data parallelism and minimizes memory access overhead in SMMO applications.  Our studies on five benchmark applications, comprising 45 kernels, demonstrate that these strategies lead to a significant reduction of average execution time by a factor of 14.  Our analysis also indicates that a mixture of early partitioning, dynamic partitioning, and partitioning based on grid maps are suitable methods for determining the optimal object partitioning.

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a composite of SO(10) U(1)Y and U(1)χ gauge symmetries. To incorporate dark matter into these models, we select a Higgs mixed-state fermion as the dark matter candidate, which is feasible because it does not necessarily belong to a neutral component. Consequently, even though U(1)χ is naturally broken by the veV_hu term, it remains possible for U(1)X to remain unbroken, thereby incorporating dark matter into the model. To examine the relevance of our approach, we compare it with the conventional fermion dark matter, focusing on a particular U(1)X and U(1)Y charged assignments that keeps three right-handed neutrinos singlet. Furthermore, the necessary conditions for dark matter stability are discussed in both scenarios.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability.

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing environmental conditions, even with limited knowledge of $\epsilon$-fidelity, has become a critical priority. Our research offers an innovative solution - a more efficient algorithm for solving the Maximum Marginal Probability (MARmax) problem with theoretical validation on key decision functions. Specifically, we've developed the first algorithm capable of solving MARmax in $n$ variables within linear computational bounds, for both symmetric and asymmetric Boolean functions. Notably, we've also devised a algorithm that solves MARmax for hypergraph and CSP problem instances in $O(2^{o(n)})$ time, improving previous solutions significantly. Our method leverages a novel and highly efficient algorithm for $\epsilon$-fidelity testing known as the Fidelity Tester, along with the concept of certified retraction.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, effectively isolating the oscillating impurity.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, it's reasonable to expect a code with a distance of four could be achieved. A proof demonstrates a code with this distance exists in the quadrangles of type W_2(q), also proving a code with a distance of six exists in the quadrangles of type W_3(q). A search for these codes a computational search, using the number of code elements, to find all possible codes with a distance of four. The search process was conducted for quadrangles of types W_1(q), W_2(9) and W_2(11). The search process revealed code families with distances of four or six, also discovering code families with a distance of eight in the quadrangles of type W_2(9).

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$, it was determined that gas density in the CMZ is significantly influenced by anisotropic spatial patterns at a scale of approximately 100 parsecs. These patterns decrease in anisotropic influence as the scale diminishes to about 10 parsecs. Our research offers a quantitative assessment of anisotropic structure in gas within the CMZ and provides a method for comparing similar regions in various areas of the galaxy.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic processes close to the Fermi level.

To develop an enhanced understanding of electronic dynamics under high-fluence conditions, researchers have created a theoretical model. This model accounts for rapid relaxation mechanisms such as electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions, treating it within the framework of the Lindblad equation for density matrix description. The model also incorporates relaxation through into the unoccupied states, interband coupling, and scattering induced by the electromagnetic pulse, all of which have been substantiated by experimental data.

The empirical evidence from the experiment aligns with the theoretical model, demonstrating that valence electrons on the few-femtosecond timescale can be promoted to the conduction band in comparable numbers, contrary to what was previously believed. The ability to promote valence electrons on such a fast timescale could significantly expand applications in the generation of carrier populations in novel ultrafast driving schemes.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a standard CMOS process to simultaneously measure temperature and supply voltage, offering a compact and efficient solution suitable for a broad range of applications. Notably, this design can detect even minor voltage fluctuations in deeply-depleted substrates that can significantly affect temperature readings. As a result, the temperature sensor is capable of detecting subtle changes in voltage that are unattainable through conventional means.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures detectability upon demand. The proposed technique is grounded in the combined effects of spontaneous four-wave mixing in a hot ensemble and classical manipulation of the pump's temporal mode. By controlling the pump's coherence and utilizing a modulated pump-bounded common-mode loss mechanism, polarization entanglement is generated through a classical pathway. The proposed method demonstrates high scalability and entanglement rates comparable to leading techniques, previously confined to optical networks and Bell inequality tests.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve previously known competitive ratios but allow for Steiner points to be added to substantially improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε. However, the authors also prove that eliminating the dependence on n in dimensions d ≥ 2 is not possible, while providing improved lower bounds under the L_1 norm: Ω(ε^(-2)/log ε^(-1)) in the plane and Ω(ε^(-d)) in R^d for d≥3.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has explored using machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices based on network traffic, with recent focus shifting to employing machine learning classifiers pre-trained on general data sets. However, this shift in focus raises questions about the fairness of classifying devices solely based on extracted network features. To address this, we conduct a preliminary study on the cost of extracting network features, with the aim of offering IoT device owners and administrators insight into their device features. Our work utilizes'state-of-the-art' feature extractors and generates a cost matrix based on the likelihood of devices sharing the same feature profile. The resulting cost matrix reveals that certain feature extractors are unfair to certain devices, with our analysis indicating that using these feature extractors may violate device owners' rights to privacy. Moreover, we reveal that leaching the pre-trained classifiers results in significantly reduced accuracy, with our experiments indicating leaching is a compromised solution compared to retraining classifiers from scratch using IoT data. Our research yields two key contributions: (i) the first to examine the cost of network features in IoT device categorization, and (ii) the first to link network feature costs with machine learning classifier fairness, with our study laying the groundwork for subsequent studies on the linked costs and fairness of feature extractors, leaching, and retraining classifiers.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of finite Godel algebras, specifically those satisfying additional conditions, and their relationship to modal Godel algebras. Additionally, the study investigates relational semantics in the form of forests with designated points. These semantics serve as morphic closed classes of finite forests, providing upper and lower bounds on modal operations. The research applies the forest duality to finite modal Godel algebras, which yields an dual representation theorem. The study also examines topological and modal Tarski semantics using continuous functions on compactly many-valued topological spaces, a type of Kripke model. The research shows that every finite modal Godel algebra can be represented as a topological modal Godel algebra, which demonstrates that the first-order part of the logic is complete.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in terms of alignment metrics, such as accuracy or F-score, our approach delivers results equivalent to GIZA++ when trained on a dataset 22 times smaller. Crucially, the method's domain-agnostic training capabilities enable 'on-the-fly' application on any new pair of sentences without requiring extensive retraining.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. With a specified mean PBH mass, our analysis suggests that primordial black holes could produce about 4 times more microlensing events than stellar black holes. Our study predicts that a planned astronomical survey will likely detect a thousand times the number of these hypothetical black hole-related microlensing events.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below $0.5$, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded $0.5$, two distinct non-standard polar crystalline phases emerged alongside the non-polar hexagonal crystal structure, namely the antiferroelectric splay crystal and the ferroelectric splay crystal. In order to study all of these configurations, we evaluated their characteristics in terms of the parameters representing nematic, smectic, and hexatic ordering. Moreover, the results of our investigations into the dynamics of these systems revealed the ferroelectric polar ordering to be stable, even in the presence of strong dynamic correlations that tended to diminish the intensity of polar ordering.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, particularly zonal functions, are well-established on the real line and non-compact real manifolds. However, these have also been identified for the sphere, although the proof that a positive definite zonal function can be represented as a Gegenbauer polynomial expansion with non-negative coefficients is long-overdue. The reason for the delay lies in the fact that standard proof techniques encounter difficulties in the spatial smoothness is not a crucial factor. The use of interpolation theory and a specialized technique to establish a linear operator's positive definiteness provides the missing link. This allows a positive definite zonal function to be represented as a Gegenbauer polynomial expansion with non-negative coefficients. Additionally, a Fourier type Banach space is formed by integrating zonal functions, enabling a positive definite zonal function to be characterized as having a Gegenbauer polynomial expansion with non-negative coefficients.

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for applications involving only light reflection and the detection of biovibrations. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an approach that converts biovibrations into spatial optical patterns. This technique utilizes an ordinary diffraction grating to transform reflections from a fixed pattern into detectable light. The process offers the ability to choose the spectrum of biovibration frequencies and can be applied to multiple vibration patterns. The technique's effectiveness has been demonstrated using a specific vibration frequency and pattern; yet, its potential exists for utilization with a wide range of frequencies and patterns.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at lower shear rates where friction is largely determined by stick-slip behavior. To gain a deeper understanding of this phenomenon, we conducted an in-depth study of the flow of polystyrene and glycerol over surfaces with designed roughness. Our results demonstrate that there are three primary states of friction: static friction which is inherent to stick-slip behavior, a regime characterized by complete surface stickage, and a regime characterized by localized stickage. The transition from the static to the complete stickage regime is accurately described by the Edgeworth approximation, while the transition from the complete to localized stickage regime is affected by complex forces originating from Van der Waals, capillary, and surface tension. Furthermore, we observed two distinct types of localized stickage: stickage along the length of the surface and stickage at the edges. The probability of stickage along the length of the surface can be predicted by considering random distribution and the probability of stickage at the edges is determined by surface roughness defects. Our research indicates that complex forces are responsible for localized stickage and therefore, the dynamic behavior of complex liquids is determined by surface micro-roughness.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate image and metadata information. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and combining image and metadata were highly effective.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on the Hertzian model, particularly woodpile chains and diatomic chains. These solitary waves emerge from the interior of the chain when a compressive force is applied to the system. Through the application of the homoclinic modulation method, we analyze the existence of nanoptera in these systems. Our calculations accurately predict both upper and lower bounds for the amplitude of nanoptera and confirm their detection via numerical integration. We observe that nanoptera are stable over an expansive range of parameters and find that their occurrence is not limited to the equilibrium configuration, as they can also be seen when the chain is not at its natural spacing. Moreover, nanoptera are stable in woodpile chains and exhibit oscillations in diatomic chains. Furthermore, our research shows that nanoptera are stable in woodpile chains and exhibit oscillations in diatomic chains. Additionally, we derive an inequality that predicts the maximum amplitude of nanoptera and, in the case of diatomic chains, we calculate the oscillation frequency of solitary waves.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. We find that a specified family of infinite quartic (also circulant) graphs that possess the PH-property belong to the general class of accordion graphs. The paper delves into the properties of accordion graphs in terms of pairings, which sometimes coincide with perfect matchings of G, and examines their close relationship with the Cartesian product of two cycles. Recent findings by Bogdanowicz have prompted a complete characterization of accordion graphs that are circulant graphs. In fact, it can be determined that A[n,k] is non-circulant if both n and k are even and k is 4 or greater.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes in self-supervised learning. Furthermore, we demonstrate the semantic segmentation capabilities of our model, showing its superiority to other self-supervised methods on semantic segmentation benchmarks.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their ability to accurately generate realistic images and perform complex image editing tasks. However, these models typically require multiple steps within an image loop to complete image generation or editing. In response, researchers proposed the Segmentation Guided Generation method, which utilizes a segment of the image area to facilitate faster processing. We introduce an alternative approach, SEGA, which stands for "Semantic Guidance through Auxiliary", based on a novel auxiliary model that streamlines image generation and editing tasks under a single unified framework. Our auxiliary model learns to identify and encode relevant semantic segments within an image, which are then utilized to guide the generative diffusion process. By leveraging these encoded semantic segments, SEGA achieves significant time savings, reducing the number of steps required for image generation and editing tasks. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate the versatility of SEGA in tackling a wide range of tasks, including top-down image generation from selected regions, bottom-up image completion from surrounding context, and even out-of-distribution generation of novel categories. We visualize the semantic segments predicted by our auxiliary model, showing that they accurately represent the underlying structure of the image, thereby enabling various tasks to be performed directly on these segments.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy neutrino oscillation experiments as sensitivity probes. We analyzed data from the CHOOZ and Double-Chooz experiments regarding neutrino oscillations in long-range travels and found that J/ψ decay into invisible matter could be a more sensitive method for detecting light sterile neutrinos than current neutrino experiments. Similarly, in the case of sub-GeV dark matter, our research shows that J/ψ decay into invisible matter offers a more precise method for detecting dark matter than current neutrino and proton fixed-target experiments, with an additional condition however that the dark matter coupling to charged leptons is greater than 10^-2 in magnitude.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of point density versus size or speed. The findings indicate that these characteristics exhibit a distinctively different statistical distributions, with point densities decreasing as size or speed increases, more pronounced in the SOT/Hinode data, and more extensively present in the HiFI/GREGOR data, spanning a wider range of scales. The fittings of the distributions to different probability functions show that the Lorentzian distribution provides the best fit, with speed and diameter patterns also fitted with a Lorentzian distribution, and area patterns with a mixture of Lorentzian and exponential distributions. The widespread presence of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere is likely due to the widespread and persistent magnetic field, persistent for a time frame of around an hour or more, as observed in the studied data, with a significant fraction having higher speeds.
